messages:
From: Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.com>
To: Samantha Cole <samantha.cole@finlytics.com>, Tom Reyes <tom.reyes@finlytics.com>
Cc: Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>, Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 03 May 2027 14:05:00 +0000
Subject: SLO clarifications + context-window implications (post-demo follow-up)

Hi Samantha / Tom —

Thanks again for your time this afternoon and for walking through the demo. Quick recap and a few clarifying questions so we can scope the next steps and provide an accurate latency/throughput projection: 

Call recap (high level):
- Finlytics will use our API to power both short interactive queries (support chat) and long-document summarization in batch-mode for nightly runs.
- Two major modes: interactive (low-latency streaming responses) and batch (high throughput, larger context windows).

Clarifying items we need to validate SLOs and estimate resource needs:
1) Latency targets: you mentioned p50 target ~150–200ms for short prompts. Can you confirm p95 and p99 goals for interactive queries?
2) Concurrency: what's the expected concurrent interactive sessions at peak? You said "hundreds" — we need a numeric target (e.g., 200 / 500 / 1k).
3) Streaming behavior: should streaming partial tokens be delivered every ~200ms or is a chunked-per-sentence approach ok? Also, maximum tolerated time-to-first-token (TTFT)?
4) Context window: please confirm max input tokens for long-document summarization and expected max output tokens. You mentioned 16k input as a ballpark — is that correct?
5) Batch throughput: for nightly jobs, what's the target docs-per-hour and average tokens per doc?

Attachments: I attached an initial SLO x context comparison matrix (slo_context_matrix.xlsx) to help you see tradeoffs between latency and token limits.

Next steps we propose:
- You confirm the numeric values above (latency p95/p99, concurrency peak, streaming TTFT, exact input/output token limits, batch throughput).
- We'll run a short projection (latency + cost) for two configuration options: hosted multi-tenant with optimized batch profiles, and a Dedicated capacity canary (reserved GPUs) with 8-bit quantized model variant for cost/latency tradeoffs.

If you can reply with the numbers today or tomorrow morning we’ll have a projection and recommended config by EOD Wed.

Thanks —
Marcus Lin
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
marcus.lin@redwood.com

On Mon, May 3, 2027 at 14:05, Marcus Lin <marcus.lin@redwood.com> wrote:
> Hi Samantha / Tom —
> 
> Thanks again for your time this afternoon and for walking through the demo. Quick recap and a few clarifying questions so we can scope the next steps and provide an accurate latency/throughput projection: 

Thanks Marcus — good recap. Answers below (numbers are approximate but accurate enough for projection):

1) Latency targets:
- Interactive (support chat): p50 ≤ 200ms (goal), p95 ≤ 450ms, p99 ≤ 900ms. The p99 is soft but we'd like it under 1s if possible.

2) Concurrency:
- Peak concurrent users for interactive support: 500 concurrent chat sessions (we measure session as an open websocket with occasional messages).

3) Streaming:
- We need streaming partial responses for the chat flow. Prefer frequent small chunks (roughly every 150–250ms) so the UI can show tokens incrementally. Time-to-first-token target: ≤ 250ms.

4) Context window:
- Long-doc summarization: typical input up to 16k tokens, occasionally spikes to 24k (we can chunk, but single-pass is preferred).
- Expected max output tokens for a summary: ~3k–4k tokens. For ad-hoc exports we might want up to 6k.

5) Batch throughput:
- Nightly job: ~4k docs over a 3-hour window (~1.3k docs/hour). Average tokens per doc ~10k (after extraction).

Notes on tolerance/tradeoffs:
- For long outputs (4k–6k tokens) we can accept higher tail latency (p95 up to 2–3s) if the interactive flows remain snappy.
- Cost sensitivity: we are evaluating Dedicated if per-token cost and predictable latency justify it.

Let us know if you need more precision. Happy to jump on a quick sync tomorrow if useful.

—Samantha
Head of Product, Finlytics
Samantha.Cole@finlytics.com

Subject: Re: SLO clarifications + context-window implications (post-demo follow-up)

Thanks Samantha — that's very helpful. Quick internal summary and recommended next steps (tagging Dev for infra input):

Implications from Finlytics numbers:
- Interactive path: 500 concurrency with p95 ≤ 450ms and TTFT ≤ 250ms requires low-latency routing, small batch sizes for short prompts, and prioritized KV / prefix cache for conversational state.
- Streaming cadence (~150–250ms) means we should avoid large aggregation buffers on the edge; prefer micro-batching + early flush.
- Long-doc summarization (16k–24k input, up to 6k output): expect significantly higher CPU/GPU time per request; tolerate higher p95/p99. Batch jobs (~1.3k docs/hr) can be scheduled on reserved nodes to improve cost predictability.

Redwood configuration options to propose:
1) Hosted optimized: multi-tenant with dynamic batching, aggressive prefix caching, and streaming-first path. Good for quick start; cheaper up-front but potential variability in tail latencies.
2) Dedicated canary (recommended for evaluation): reserved GPU pool (x4 A100-equivalent nodes), pinned model variant (q8_4bit or similar), canary for 8 weeks, run both interactive and nightly batch on separate node pools. Provides predictable p95/p99 and easier SLAs.

Action items / ask list:
- Marcus: send formal proposal comparing the two options (latency projections, cost estimates).
- Dev: can you prepare a preliminary latency projection for q8 quantized variant (attached CSV) and confirm whether 150–250ms streaming intervals are achievable with our micro-batching strategy?
- Samantha: confirm whether occasional 24k inputs are mandatory single-pass or if chunking is acceptable for those edge cases.

I'll draft a short one-pager for execs that maps performance profiles to expected monthly cost and SLA delta. Marcus — can you schedule a 30-minute follow-up for tomorrow morning PT?

Thanks —
Lauren Bishop
Director, Solutions — Redwood Inference

From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: SLO clarifications + context-window implications (post-demo follow-up)

Hi all — quick technical clarifications so our projection matches your expectations: 

1) Tail targets: Are the p99 goals for interactive flows hard constraints or acceptance thresholds? For planning I'd treat p95 ≤ 450ms as our engineering SLO and p99 ≤ 900ms as a contractual target (we can refine).

2) Streaming chunking: We'll aim for early-first-token ≤ 250ms and then micro-chunks every ~200ms. Can you confirm the UI can handle updates at ~200ms cadence vs larger 500ms chunks?

3) Long inputs: If single-pass 24k is non-negotiable, our cost + latency projection increases substantially. If chunking (sliding window or chunk+stitch) is allowed for >16k spikes, projections improve and we can keep tail latency targets lower.

4) Autoscaling and concurrency model: We'll propose two autoscaling profiles — one optimized for interactive (fast scale with warm pools) and one for batch (capacity-scheduled windows). Need to know how much pre-warm capacity you'd accept as reserved for peak interactive.

I've attached an initial latency projection for our q8 pipeline (latency_projection_q8.csv) — it includes estimated p50/p95/p99 for 1k, 500, and 200 concurrent sessions across short (<=256 tokens) and long (>=4k token output) request classes.

Proposed follow-up: 30-minute technical deep-dive tomorrow 10:00 PT — Marcus, can you confirm slot? If that works we'll invite one engineer from Finlytics so we can align on exact streaming chunk sizes and how to measure TTFT from your client.

Regards,
Dev Patel
Senior Software Engineer, Infra — Redwood Inference
